text.brief: In 1998 the fundraiser Johnny Chung told federal investigators that a lieutenant colonel in the People's Liberation Army had given him $300,000 for American campaigns.
text.record: Chung said the money came from Liu Chaoying, a state aerospace executive and the daughter of the army's senior general ([House Report 105-829: Investigation of political fundraising improprieties and possible violations of law (govinfo)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CRPT-105hrpt829/pdf/CRPT-105hrpt829-vol1.pdf)). He pleaded guilty to campaign finance violations. The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee reported in 1998 that Party officials had planned to influence American elections, and its minority disputed how far the plan went ([Senate Report 105-167, Vol. 1: Investigation of illegal or improper activities in connection with 1996 federal election campaigns (Committee on Governmental Affairs)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CRPT-105srpt167/pdf/CRPT-105srpt167-pt1.pdf); [Senate Report 105-167, Vol. 6 (minority views)](https://www.congress.gov/105/crpt/srpt167/CRPT-105srpt167-pt6.pdf)). The Democratic National Committee returned about $2.8 million in questionable donations and then called donors with Asian surnames to question their citizenship ([House Report 105-829, Vol. 1: Investigation of political fundraising improprieties (govinfo)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CRPT-105hrpt829/pdf/CRPT-105hrpt829-vol1.pdf)).
text.reading: The Party ran money through a few intermediaries, and suspicion then fell on every American who shared their ancestry. That second result served the Party as well as the first, because it taught Asian Americans that their own institutions saw them as suspects.
text.gapText: Architecture Governance. No one owned the source of foreign money that reached campaigns through citizens, so scrutiny fell on ancestry instead of on money.
text.fix: Trace the money rather than the donor's name, and apply the same test to every contribution.
